content: Certain stabilizers used in Dangerous Goods classified as Class 3 (alcohols), Class 8 (formaldehydes), or Class 9 may meet the criteria for Dangerous Goods packed in excepted quantities. In such cases, stabilizers present in the primary container in quantities of 30 mL or less are exempt from additional requirements of their dangerous goods classification, provided they are packaged according to UN model regulations P620 or P650. The term overpack refers to the practice of combining multiple packages into a single unit for shipment to the same destination by one shipper. If dry ice is used to protect the contents, the overpacks may include insulated vessels or flasks that allow carbon dioxide gas to dissipate, such as through clear plastic wrapping. Packaging materials can be reused or returned to the consignor, but they must first be disinfected or sterilized to eliminate any hazards. Any labels or markings indicating the packaging previously contained infectious substances must be removed or obscured. Reused packaging must also comply with quality testing standards for Category A and B packaging. If the packaging is damaged or weakened, it should no longer be used. Stabilizers may inactivate certain biological agents, rendering them non-infectious to humans or animals. In such cases, professional judgment may allow the substance to be reclassified as exempt. Once the appropriate packaging materials are assembled, they must be clearly marked and labeled to indicate the contents, the nature of the hazard, and the applicable packaging standards. Labels must be visible and not obscured by other markings. For example, if dry ice is used, the UN number and proper shipping name of the coolant must be followed by the words AS COOLANT. For Category A infectious substances, additional markings are required, including the UN packaging symbol, certification marks, and the name and telephone number of a knowledgeable contact person. The net quantity of the substance refers to the total amount inside the package, excluding the weight of packaging or coolant materials. This information is critical for maintaining cold chain conditions during transit and for biosafety risk assessments in case of spillage or leakage. For Category B infectious substances, specific markings must be displayed, such as a square symbol with minimum dimensions and contrasting colors. The proper shipping name Biological Substance, Category B must be displayed adjacent to the mark. Hazard labels for infectious substances must meet specific design and size requirements, such as a diamond shape with a white background and black writing. For Category A substances, the label must include the inscription INFECTIOUS SUBSTANCE and instructions to notify public health authorities in case of damage or leakage. Additional labels may be required for coolants like dry ice or cryogenic liquids. For infectious substances, these labels are mandatory for packages containing more than 50 mL of liquid. Cargo aircraft-only labels are required for packages exceeding passenger aircraft quantity limits. Cryogenic liquid warning labels must also be used when applicable. Transport documentation, such as a Dangerous Goods Transport Document (DGTD), is required for Category A infectious substances and certain medical or clinical wastes. However, Category B substances packaged according to P650 are exempt from this requirement. The DGTD must include information about the sender, receiver, date, description of the goods, handling requirements, emergency response information, and certification by the shipper. Emergency response information must be available for personnel in case of packaging breaches. Spill clean-up procedures include wearing protective clothing, covering the spill with absorbent material, applying disinfectant, and safely disposing of contaminated materials. The incident must be reported to the competent authority after decontamination. An air waybill is a standard shipping document required for all goods transported by air, including infectious substances. It must include details about the shipper, receiver, and the nature and quantity of the goods. For exempt specimens, the phrase exempt specimens should be included. If shipped with coolant, the proper shipping name, UN number, and net quantity of the coolant must also be provided. Special provisions may apply to certain shipments of infectious substances, such as exemptions for aqueous solutions with low alcohol content or genetically modified organisms packaged according to specific instructions. Air transport-specific provisions include exemptions for body parts or organs and requirements for venting carbon dioxide gas when dry ice is used as a refrigerant.
